title: Evaluating an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM-Generated Network Changes
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We expand methodological detail, provide a compact formal definition of the binary scoring rule with a concrete artifact-grounded example, add a concise nearest-work comparison matrix, condense provenance to a compact artifact paragraph, and discuss construct/external validity limits and design recommendations for future confirmatory studies.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent into concrete device commands, but syntactically plausible outputs may violate stateful workflow invariants (for example, performing a VLAN or MTU change without a required shutdown step). Prior work therefore argues for integrating verification, emulation, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. We designed a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) to isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. Research question: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? Our primary contribution is an artifact-rich paired experiment that holds the generator fixed and measures validator/repair influence on identical candidates, together with a concise formalization of the binary scoring rule used for confirmatory testing and a nearest-work comparison that clarifies what this design isolates versus previous generator-focused evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Two research strands motivate our design. First, executable emulation and closed-loop NetOps benchmarks (e.g., NetConfArena and related executable-benchmark efforts) demonstrate that token-level correctness need not imply safe enactment: closed-loop execution surfaces sequencing and stateful errors such as make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, and ordered-operation requirements. Second, tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) are repeatedly proposed to reduce operational risk. Prior empirical studies commonly conflate generator variability and verifier efficacy because they compare pipelines where generation and verification are both free to vary. Our shared-generation paired design removes generator variance across paired episodes and measures the validator/repair subsystem's marginal effect.

Nearest-work comparison (compact). The table below summarizes how the closest prior experiments differ from this study along the dimensions most relevant to confirmatory inference: shared-generation paired design, use of an executable emulator validator, explicit repair budget, synthetic/deterministic task corpus, and single hosted LLM model. Source identifiers are verified in the archived bibliography.

Nearest-work matrix (summary):
- Protogeros et al., "Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair" (arXiv:2604.22513): typical generator-focused benchmarks; executable evaluation present but studies do not use a shared-generation paired design (Shared-generation: No; Executable validator: Yes; Repair budget explicit: No; Synthetic deterministic corpus: Partial; Single model: No).
- Liu et al., "NetConfArena" (arXiv:2608.23179): closed-loop executable benchmark emphasizing end-to-end behavior (Shared-generation: No; Executable validator: Yes; Repair budget explicit: No; Synthetic deterministic corpus: Yes; Single model: No).
- Zhou et al., "MeshAgent" (SIG): agentic system evaluating reliability in managed pipelines (Shared-generation: No; Executable validator: Partial; Repair budget explicit: Partial; Synthetic deterministic corpus: Partial; Single model: No).
- Tang et al., "Lightyear" (SIGCOMM work on verification): verification-focused (Shared-generation: No; Executable validator: Yes; Repair budget explicit: No; Synthetic deterministic corpus: No; Single model: No).

This compact comparison locates our study as validator-focused (shared-generation paired design) and preregistered with an explicit repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), emphasizing different causal claims than generator-centered benchmarks.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. The preregistration specified a paired confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned into three fixed topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine, 40 tasks each). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified test was the exact two-sided McNemar. A bootstrap-percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729. The preregistered repair budget capped repair iterations at ≤1 per guarded episode. Planned vs completed episodes and provider-call audits are archived.

Task generation and harness. Tasks were deterministically generated (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest includes initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, a required_sequence (canonical ordered steps), and difficulty metadata. To isolate validator effects we applied a shared-generation paired design: each pair used one shared initial candidate produced by the declared model (gpt-5-mini). The execution manifest reports model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator that enforces structured workflow policies (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator executes the candidate in an emulated state checker and emits a structured validator_trace containing validation_before/after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. Per preregistered policy, a single repair iteration could be requested when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and traces would be archived. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and repair_applied = false across the dataset.

Compact provenance paragraph (condensed). Key archived artifacts required to reproduce confirmatory accounting are provided in the execution and analysis bundles: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/*, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Representative artifact hashes and the full execution manifest are archived with the study; detailed provenance manifests are available in the artifact bundle referenced by the preregistration id CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1. This paragraph intentionally replaces longer inline inventories with compact file-name references to preserve readability while keeping machine-verifiable artifacts available in the archive.

Formal, compact binary scoring rule (required revision resolved). The confirmatory test used a deterministic binary pass/fail mapping from the validator/scorer artifacts to a paired outcome per task. We report the rule here precisely and give an artifact-grounded example.

Scoring rule (formal): For each episode (baseline or guarded), define PASS iff all of the following hold in the episode's scoring artifact (execution/scoring/task-<id>-*.json):
1) scorer.score == 1 AND scorer.score_reason_code == "VALID_CONFIGURATION"; AND
2) validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true; AND
3) validator_trace.violation_count == 0.
If any condition is false or missing, label the episode FAIL. The paired binary label for McNemar is PASS/FAIL based on the episode-level mapping.

Concrete example (artifact-grounded): execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json contains scorer.score = 1, score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count = 0; therefore task-000001-baseline is labeled PASS under the formal rule. The same episode's guarded artifact (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) shows identical fields and is also labeled PASS. Representative artifacts for other tasks (e.g., task-000002, task-000003) follow the same schema and are archived.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared initial generation per pair). Condition-level summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0, guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes, so the preregistered repair endpoint is vacuous in this run.

Per-topology counts. The deterministic partition produced 40 tasks per topology class. Counts per archived scoring artifacts and analysis/condition_summary.csv are:
- Edge: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40 PASS, guarded 40/40 PASS.
- Core: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40 PASS, guarded 40/40 PASS.
- Leaf–spine: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40 PASS, guarded 40/40 PASS.

Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts (for example execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) show: normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer; parsed_command_count equals required_command_count from the task payload; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.repair_applied = false; validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator_version = 5.0. These artifacts show that the generator satisfied the task-encoded structured constraints for the sampled task bank and prompt strategy.

Contamination and reconciliation. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero exclusions. deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms provider-call audit counts and pair accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120, cross-condition cache reuse = false).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The preregistered shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by holding the generator fixed; it therefore answers the narrow mechanistic question of whether a validator/repair subsystem can improve outcomes for identical generator outputs. In the archived task bank and prompt configuration the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs, so the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair and hence could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling outcome.

Design recommendations grounded in archived difficulty metadata. The task_manifest difficulty fields (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) and the observed absence of repairs suggest concrete preregistered adjustments for future confirmatory work: (1) allow independent per-condition generation in one confirmatory arm to expose generation variance; (2) prespecify targeted subsets of tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count to increase generator-induced violation incidence; (3) include controlled prompt perturbations on a prespecified fraction of tasks; (4) expand repair budget in exploratory arms to study repair convergence dynamics. These adjustments are implementable using the archived task_manifest selections without changing harness semantics.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator's policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; the validator enforces canonical required_sequence checks but does not emulate all vendor-specific behaviors. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure ≈0.40 and targeted an absolute reduction of 0.15; observed baseline = 0.00 violates those assumptions and renders the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.

Operational implications. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts demonstrate end-to-end instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) useful for operator explanations and third-party audits in deployments where generators sometimes err. The empirical lesson is methodological: experimental framing must ensure the generator produces enough invalid candidates (for example via task selection or perturbation) for a validator/repair subsystem to have an opportunity to demonstrate measurable benefit.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and illustrates that the shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
